Disorders","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":249,"printedEnd":256,"pdfStart":267,"pdfEnd":274,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"Parkinson’s disease and Huntington’s disease illustrate how motor disorders arise from different changes in neural systems. Their symptoms extend beyond overt movement and can affect cognition and everyday functioning."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The book examines mechanisms, heredity, prediction, and treatment. Keep the distinction between reducing symptoms and reversing a disease process clear when studying the available interventions."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-3-study-1","text":"Parkinson’s disease"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Parkinson’s disease commonly involves slowed initiation of movement, rigidity, and tremor, although symptom patterns vary. Loss of dopamine-producing neurons that project to basal ganglia circuits disrupts the regulation of movement. Because the affected networks influence more than movement, people may also experience other changes. Understanding the relevant circuit is more informative than saying only that dopamine is 'low': the consequences depend on which pathways receive altered dopamine signaling."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-3-study-2","text":"Treatments and their limits"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"L-Dopa provides a precursor from which the brain can produce dopamine and can reduce important movement symptoms. Other treatments may alter dopaminergic signaling, and selected patients may benefit from approaches such as deep-brain stimulation. Rehabilitation and other non-drug interventions can support function. None of these methods is a simple cure that reverses every aspect of the underlying process. Treatment decisions depend on individual benefits, side effects, and stage of illness."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-3-study-3","text":"Huntington’s disease"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Huntington’s disease is a hereditary condition that affects movement and additional aspects of behavior and cognition. It is associated with a mutation in the huntingtin gene. Because its inheritance pattern carries implications for family members, genetic testing raises questions about predicting disease risk in someone who does not yet show symptoms. Presymptomatic testing requires careful understanding of what a result can and cannot tell a person."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-3-study-4","text":"Compare the two disorders"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Both disorders implicate basal ganglia networks, but they differ in characteristic movements, biology, and inheritance. Parkinson’s often emphasizes difficulty initiating and controlling movements; Huntington’s can involve unwanted movements alongside other changes. Avoid the misconception that a movement disorder is 'only a motor problem.' The effects of disrupted circuits can extend into motivation, emotion, and thinking."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-3-h01","text":"Parkinson’s Disease"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Parkinson’s disease results from the gradual loss of dopamine-releasing axons going from the substantia nigra to the striatum.","sourcePrintedPage":249,"sourcePdfPage":267,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"genetically defined type of dopamine neuron in a limited portion of the substantia nigra .","sourcePrintedPage":249,"sourcePdfPage":267,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disease—one that gradually progresses to a worse and worse outcome.","sourcePrintedPage":249,"sourcePdfPage":267,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It affects more than 1 percent of people over age 60, with increasing prevalence at higher ages.","sourcePrintedPage":249,"sourcePdfPage":267,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with Parkinson’s disease sometimes move normally in response to signals or instructions, such as while following a parade , but their spontaneous, self-initiated movements are slow and weak.","sourcePrintedPage":249,"sourcePdfPage":267,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many, but not all, Parkinson’s patients may experience depression , and many have problems with attention, language, or memory .","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-3-h02","text":"Causes"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Early-onset Parkinson’s disease (usually defined as before age 40 to 50) has high heritability, but the far more common late-onset condition has lower heritability .","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers have identified genes that can cause early-onset Parkinson’s disease, and many genetic variants that slightly raise the risk of late-onset Parkinson’s disease .","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Having a brother or sister with the condition increases the risk more than does having a parent or child with the condition .","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The pattern of results indicates that genes contribute to the risk, but factors in the environment might be even more important, especially for late-onset Parkinson’s.","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The substance responsible for the symptoms was MPTP , a chemical that the body converts to MPP 1 , which accumulates in, and then destroys, neurons that release dopamine 1 .","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"No one supposes that Parkinson’s disease often results from using recreational drugs, but much research suggests increased risk among workers with much exposure to pesticides (e.g., farmers) or metals (welders and miners) .","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Exposure to harmful chemicals increases the risk especially among people with any of the genes that predispose to Parkinson’s .","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In contrast, 13.8 percent of the smokers developed the disease, as did only 11.6 percent of the heaviest smokers .","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-3-h03","text":"L-Dopa Treatment"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because Parkinson’s disease results from a dopamine deficiency, a logical goal is to restore the missing dopamine.","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A dopamine pill would be ineffective because dopamine does not cross the blood–brain barrier.","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Physicians in the 1950s and 1960s reasoned that L-dopa , a precursor to dopamine that does cross the barrier, might be a good treatment.","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In contrast to all the medicines that were discovered by trial and error, this was the first drug in psychiatry or neurology, and one of the first in all of medicine, to emerge from a plausible theory.","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Taken as a daily pill, L-dopa reaches the brain, where neurons convert it to dopamine, partially restoring movement and other behaviors.","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They are more effective in some people than in others, probably because of variation in the intestinal bacteria that metabolize L-dopa before it can enter the blood .","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The side effects are usually tolerable, but they can include nausea, restlessness, sleep problems, low blood pressure, repetitive movements, and sometimes hallucinations and delusions.","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-3-h04","text":"Non-pharmaceutical Therapies"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If dopamine replacement becomes ineffective or unsatisfactory, physicians sometimes implant electrodes to stimulate the subthalamic nucleus or the globus pallidus.","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The stimulation facilitates desired movements and inhibits unintended movements .","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One hypothesis is that people with Parkinson’s disease have excessive synchrony of firing in the basal ganglia, and the stimulation breaks up unhealthy rhythms .","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The limitation has been that continuous brain stimulation drains the battery attached to the electrodes.","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Basic research on the basal ganglia revealed that the electrical stimulation stimulates two types of neurons with different effects.","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"So far, this procedure has been tried only with laboratory mice, but it has much potential for use with humans .","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Control animals that suffered the same brain damage without receiving grafts showed little or no recovery.","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This is only a partial brain transplant, but still, the Frankensteinian implications are striking.","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Fetal neurons transplanted into the brain of patients with Parkinson’s sometimes survive for years and make synapses with the patients’ own cells.","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, the operation is expensive and difficult, requiring brain tissue from four to eight fetuses aborted at just the right stage of development.","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-3-h05","text":"Huntington’s Disease"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Huntington’s disease is a severe neurological disorder that affects about 17 per 100,000 Americans of European ancestry, less than half that many Europeans in Europe itself, probably fewer Africans—although the data for Africa are sparse—and very few Asians .","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Motor symptoms usually begin with arm jerks and facial twitches that gradually spread to other parts of the body and develop into writhing.","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the output from the basal ganglia is inhibitory to the thalamus, damage to the basal ganglia leads to increased activity in parts of the thalamus, producing the involuntary jerky movements.","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with Huntington’s disease also suffer psychological disorders including apathy, depression, sleeplessness, memory impairment, anxiety, hallucinations and delusions, poor judgment, alcoholism, drug abuse, and sexual disorders ranging from complete unresponsiveness to indiscriminate promiscuity .","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Huntington’s disease can have onset at any age, but most often between the ages of 30 and 50.","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Like Parkinson’s disease, Huntington’s is a progressive disease.","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-3-h06","text":"Heredity and Presymptomatic Testing"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Of all the conditions we consider in this text other than color vision deficiency, Huntington’s disease is the only one that can be traced to a single gene.","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"That gene is an autosomal dominant gene (i.e., not on the X or Y chromosome).","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"As a rule, a mutant gene that causes the loss of a function is recessive.","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The fact that the Huntington’s gene is dominant implies that it produces the gain of an undesirable function.","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most people who are at risk choose not to be tested, and about half of those who do get tested do not return to the clinic to learn the results.","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"As is often the case, people try to avoid threatening or unpleasant information .","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The critical area of the gene is a sequence of bases C-A-G (cytosine, adenine, guanine), repeated 11 to 24 times in most people.","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"That repetition produces a string of 11 to 24 glutamines in the resulting protein.","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with more repetitions are nearly certain to get the disease, unless they die of other causes earlier.","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The mutant form impairs neurons and glia in several ways, including effects on mitochondria and potassium channels .","sourcePrintedPage":253,"sourcePdfPage":271,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the early stages of the disease, it increases neurotransmitter release, sometimes causing overstimulation of the target cells .","sourcePrintedPage":253,"sourcePdfPage":271,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Identifying the abnormal huntingtin protein and its cellular functions has enabled investigators to search for drugs that might be helpful.","sourcePrintedPage":253,"sourcePdfPage":271,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"After this loss of input, the striatum decreases its inhibition of the globus pallidus, which therefore increases its inhibitory input to the thalamus, as depicted in Figure 7.20.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h01","sourcePrintedPage":249,"sourcePdfPage":267},{"type":"bullet","text":"The symptoms include rigidity, muscle tremors, slow movements, and difficulty initiating voluntary activity.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h01","sourcePrintedPage":249,"sourcePdfPage":267},{"type":"bullet","text":"The genetic similarity is the same, but brother and sister have their early environment in common.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h02","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268},{"type":"bullet","text":"One study found many cases in which both husband and wife developed Parkinson’s disease.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h02","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268},{"type":"bullet","text":"When researchers compared the lifestyles of people who did and didn’t develop the disease, they found that people who smoke cigarettes or drink coffee or tea have less chance of developing Parkinson’s disease.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h02","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268},{"type":"bullet","text":"(Consider that sentence again.) One study took questionnaire results from more than a thousand pairs of young adult twins and compared the results to medical records decades later.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h02","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268},{"type":"bullet","text":"L-dopa is still the most common treatment for Parkinson’s disease.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h03","sourcePrintedPage":250,"sourcePdfPage":268},{"type":"bullet","text":"Other treatments include drugs that directly stimulate dopamine receptors and drugs that stimulation.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h04","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269},{"type":"bullet","text":"Perlow and colleagues (1979) injected the chemical 6-OHDA (6-hydroxydopamine, a chemical body.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h04","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269},{"type":"bullet","text":"One 59-yearold man improved dramatically, and for the next 10 years he had only minor symptoms, synapses.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h04","sourcePrintedPage":251,"sourcePdfPage":269},{"type":"bullet","text":"Gradually, the tremors interfere more and more with walking, speech, and other voluntary your mother or father has Huntington’s disease.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h06","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270},{"type":"bullet","text":"In addition to your grief about your parent, you know that you have a 50 percent chance of getting the disease yourself.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h06","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270},{"type":"bullet","text":"An examination of your chromosomes can reveal with almost perfect accuracy whether or not you will get Huntington’s disease.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h06","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270},{"type":"bullet","text":"Knowing the answer might help you decide whether to have children, whether to enter a career that required many years of education, and so forth.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h06","sourcePrintedPage":252,"sourcePdfPage":270},{"type":"bullet","text":"Evidently other factors besides genes also influence the age of onset, such as stressful experiences, drug or alcohol abuse, and perhaps diet and exercise.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h06","sourcePrintedPage":253,"sourcePdfPage":271},{"type":"bullet","text":"Each of them relates to an extended sequence of C-A-G repeats in a gene.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h06","sourcePrintedPage":253,"sourcePdfPage":271},{"type":"bullet","text":"Progress has been slow, but medications that reduce the production of the huntingtin protein have exhibited some promise.","headingId":"bp14-m7-3-h06","sourcePrintedPage":253,"sourcePdfPage":271},{"type":"bullet","text":"Parkinson’s disease and treatment.","printedPage":250,"pdfPage":268,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":29},{"text":"In contrast to all the medicines that were discovered by theory.","printedPage":250,"pdfPage":268,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":30},{"text":"Taken as a daily pill, L-dopa reaches the brain, where neurons behaviors.","printedPage":250,"pdfPage":268,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":31},{"text":"They are more effective in some people than in others, probably because of variation in the intestinal bacteria that metabolize L-dopa before it can enter the blood .","printedPage":250,"pdfPage":268,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":32},{"text":"The side effects are usually tolerable, but they can include nausea, restlessness, sleep problems, low blood pressure, repetitive movements, and sometimes hallucinations and delusions.","printedPage":250,"pdfPage":268,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":33},{"text":"L-dopa is still the most common treatment for Parkinson’s effects.","printedPage":251,"pdfPage":269,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":39},{"text":"So far, this procedure has been tried only with laboratory development.","printedPage":251,"pdfPage":269,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":44},{"text":"Researchers then found that a series of short bursts of .","printedPage":251,"pdfPage":269,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":46},{"text":"Motor symptoms usually begin with arm jerks and facial twitches that .","printedPage":253,"pdfPage":271,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":63},{"text":"Identifying the abnormal huntingtin protein and its cellular A complete understanding combines the mechanism of damage, the movement symptoms, and the person's broader daily functioning.","paragraphIndex":801906,"kind":"individually_written_classroom_explanation","level":"contextual_clarification","sourceHeadingId":"bp14-m7-3-h07","sourcePrintedPage":254,"sourcePdfPage":272,"editorialStatus":"individual_topic_specific_explanation_drafted_from_source_topic_map","evidenceBasis":"Supplied Kalat 14e PDF and matching Markdown; existing source-extracted paragraphs kept as separate verifiable references","needsIndependentReview":true}}],"classroomParagraphs":["Parkinson’s disease results from the gradual loss of dopamine-releasing axons going from the substantia nigra to the striatum.","genetically defined type of dopamine neuron in a limited portion of the substantia nigra.","Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disease—one that gradually progresses to a worse and worse outcome.","It affects more than 1 percent of people over age 60, with increasing prevalence at higher ages. People with Parkinson’s disease sometimes move normally in response to signals or instructions, such as while following a parade, but their spontaneous, self-initiated movements are slow and weak.","Many, but not all, Parkinson’s patients may experience depression, and many have problems with attention, language, or memory.","Early-onset Parkinson’s disease (usually defined as before age 40 to 50) has high heritability, but the far more common late-onset condition has lower heritability.","Researchers have identified genes that can cause early-onset Parkinson’s disease, and many genetic variants that slightly raise the risk of late-onset Parkinson’s disease.","Having a brother or sister with the condition increases the risk more than does having a parent or child with the condition. The pattern of results indicates that genes contribute to the risk, but factors in the environment might be even more important, especially for late-onset Parkinson’s.","The substance responsible for the symptoms was MPTP, a chemical that the body converts to MPP 1, which accumulates in, and then destroys, neurons that release dopamine 1.","No one supposes that Parkinson’s disease often results from using recreational drugs, but much research suggests increased risk among workers with much exposure to pesticides (e.g., farmers) or metals (welders and miners).","Exposure to harmful chemicals increases the risk especially among people with any of the genes that predispose to Parkinson’s. In contrast, 13.8 percent of the smokers developed the disease, as did only 11.6 percent of the heaviest smokers.","Because Parkinson’s disease results from a dopamine deficiency, a logical goal is to restore the missing dopamine.","A dopamine pill would be ineffective because dopamine does not cross the blood–brain barrier.","Physicians in the 1950s and 1960s reasoned that L-dopa, a precursor to dopamine that does cross the barrier, might be a good treatment. In contrast to all the medicines that were discovered by trial and error, this was the first drug in psychiatry or neurology, and one of the first in all of medicine, to emerge from a plausible theory.","Taken as a daily pill, L-dopa reaches the brain, where neurons convert it to dopamine, partially restoring movement and other behaviors.","They are more effective in some people than in others, probably because of variation in the intestinal bacteria that metabolize L-dopa before it can enter the blood. The side effects are usually tolerable, but they can include nausea, restlessness, sleep problems, low blood pressure, repetitive movements, and sometimes hallucinations and delusions.","If dopamine replacement becomes ineffective or unsatisfactory, physicians sometimes implant electrodes to stimulate the subthalamic nucleus or the globus pallidus.","The stimulation facilitates desired movements and inhibits unintended movements.","One hypothesis is that people with Parkinson’s disease have excessive synchrony of firing in the basal ganglia, and the stimulation breaks up unhealthy rhythms.","The limitation has been that continuous brain stimulation drains the battery attached to the electrodes. Basic research on the basal ganglia revealed that the electrical stimulation stimulates two types of neurons with different effects.","So far, this procedure has been tried only with laboratory mice, but it has much potential for use with humans.","Control animals that suffered the same brain damage without receiving grafts showed little or no recovery.","This is only a partial brain transplant, but still, the Frankensteinian implications are striking. Fetal neurons transplanted into the brain of patients with Parkinson’s sometimes survive for years and make synapses with the patients’ own cells.","However, the operation is expensive and difficult, requiring brain tissue from four to eight fetuses aborted at just the right stage of development.","Huntington’s disease is a severe neurological disorder that affects about 17 per 100,000 Americans of European ancestry, less than half that many Europeans in Europe itself, probably fewer Africans—although the data for Africa are sparse—and very few Asians.","Motor symptoms usually begin with arm jerks and facial twitches that gradually spread to other parts of the body and develop into writhing.","Because the output from the basal ganglia is inhibitory to the thalamus, damage to the basal ganglia leads to increased activity in parts of the thalamus, producing the involuntary jerky movements.","People with Huntington’s disease also suffer psychological disorders including apathy, depression, sleeplessness, memory impairment, anxiety, hallucinations and delusions, poor judgment, alcoholism, drug abuse, and sexual disorders ranging from complete unresponsiveness to indiscriminate promiscuity. Huntington’s disease can have onset at any age, but most often between the ages of 30 and 50.","Like Parkinson’s disease, Huntington’s is a progressive disease.","Of all the conditions we consider in this text other than color vision deficiency, Huntington’s disease is the only one that can be traced to a single gene.","That gene is an autosomal dominant gene (i.e., not on the X or Y chromosome).","As a rule, a mutant gene that causes the loss of a function is recessive. The fact that the Huntington’s gene is dominant implies that it produces the gain of an undesirable function.","Most people who are at risk choose not to be tested, and about half of those who do get tested do not return to the clinic to learn the results.","As is often the case, people try to avoid threatening or unpleasant information. The critical area of the gene is a sequence of bases C-A-G (cytosine, adenine, guanine), repeated 11 to 24 times in most people.","That repetition produces a string of 11 to 24 glutamines in the resulting protein. People with more repetitions are nearly certain to get the disease, unless they die of other causes earlier.","The mutant form impairs neurons and glia in several ways, including effects on mitochondria and potassium channels.","In the early stages of the disease, it increases neurotransmitter release, sometimes causing overstimulation of the target cells. Identifying the abnormal huntingtin protein and its cellular functions has enabled investigators to search for drugs that might be helpful.","Parkinson’s disease and Huntington’s disease result from brain deterioration that includes the basal ganglia.","Parkinson’s disease is characterized by impaired initiation of activity, slow and inaccurate movements, tremor, rigidity, depression, and cognitive deficits. Parkinson’s disease is caused by degeneration of dopamine-containing axons from the substantia nigra to the caudate nucleus and putamen.","The degeneration of dopamine axons results from both genetic of Waking and Sleeping","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":258,"printedEnd":268,"pdfStart":276,"pdfEnd":286,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sleep and waking follow endogenous circadian rhythms that are coordinated with environmental cues. The suprachiasmatic nucleus and responses to light help align the body’s clock with the outside world."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Jet lag, night work, and individual differences in daily preference illustrate what happens when biological timing and daily demands do not match. Track how clock mechanisms, melatonin, and behavior interact."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m8-1-study-1","text":"Biological rhythms are built in"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many bodily processes vary across roughly daily cycles, including alertness, hormone secretion, and temperature. Circadian rhythms are endogenous, meaning they can continue even when ordinary external time cues are absent. Nonetheless, light and daily routines help reset them to the environment. The distinction between an internal oscillator and an outside cue is essential: light usually synchronizes a system rather than creating each individual rhythm from nothing."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m8-1-study-2","text":"The suprachiasmatic nucleus"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A small hypothalamic region called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) acts as a central circadian timing system in mammals. Input related to environmental light helps adjust its timing. Molecular feedback mechanisms inside cells support recurring rhythms, and the SCN influences other neural and hormonal processes. Melatonin is associated with the night phase and can convey timing information, but it is not a substitute for understanding the whole clock system."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m8-1-study-3","text":"Jet lag, shift work, and chronotype"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Travel across time zones may abruptly change the clock time outside while internal rhythms remain closer to the old schedule. The resulting mismatch is jet lag. Night work can similarly put sleep and activity out of step with some biological timing processes. Individuals differ in whether they naturally prefer earlier or later schedules, often described as morningness and eveningness. These variations make sleep timing a biological as well as a practical issue."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m8-1-study-4","text":"What to remember about resetting"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Light exposure at different times can shift the circadian clock in different directions, so timing matters as much as amount. Other routines may contribute to synchronization, but light is a major signal. Do not confuse total hours slept with circadian alignment: a person can sleep for an adequate duration but at a biologically awkward time and still experience problems with alertness."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m8-1-h01","text":"Endogenous Rhythms"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An animal that produced its behavior entirely in response to current stimuli would be at a serious disadvantage.","sourcePrintedPage":258,"sourcePdfPage":276,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, migratory birds start flying toward their winter homes before their summer territory becomes too cold.","sourcePrintedPage":258,"sourcePdfPage":276,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A small bird that waited for the first frost would be in serious trouble.","sourcePrintedPage":258,"sourcePdfPage":276,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Similarly, squirrels begin storing nuts and putting on extra layers of fat in preparation for winter long before food becomes scarce.","sourcePrintedPage":258,"sourcePdfPage":276,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the tropics, the temperature and amount of daylight are nearly the same throughout the year.","sourcePrintedPage":258,"sourcePdfPage":276,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Even if they are kept in a cage with no clues to the season, they become restless in the spring, and if they are released, they fly north .","sourcePrintedPage":258,"sourcePdfPage":276,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Even in this unchanging environment, the animal generates a consistent rhythm of activity and sleep.","sourcePrintedPage":258,"sourcePdfPage":276,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although they try to sleep on this 18-hour schedule, their bodies generate rhythms of alertness and body chemistry that continue to average a bit more than 24 hours, and their alertness suffers .","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We have circadian rhythms in our hunger, thirst, liver activity, insulin secretion, intestinal activity, DNA repair, and much else .","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most showed increases in positive mood (happiness) from waking until late afternoon, and then a slight decline until bedtime.","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m8-1-h02","text":"Setting and Resetting the Biological Clock"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In addition to light, other zeitgebers include exercise , arousal , meals, and the temperature of the environment .","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Social stimuli—that is, the effects of other people—are ineffective as zeitgebers, unless they induce exercise or other vigorous activity .","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although these additional zeitgebers modify the effects of light, they have only weak effects.","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People who are working in Antarctica during the constant darkness of an Antarctic winter maintain an approximately 24-hour rhythm, but different people generate","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"slightly different rhythms, until they find it more and more difficult to work together .","sourcePrintedPage":260,"sourcePdfPage":278,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When we try to set our wake–sleep cycles by the clock, sunlight still has its influence.","sourcePrintedPage":260,"sourcePdfPage":278,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Particularly impressive evidence for the importance of sunlight comes from a study in Germany.","sourcePrintedPage":260,"sourcePdfPage":278,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers asked adults for their preferred times of awakening and going to sleep and determined for each person the midpoint of those values.","sourcePrintedPage":260,"sourcePdfPage":278,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, those who are not as sensitive to these secondary zeitgebers produce circadian rhythms that are a little longer than 24 hours.","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When their cycles are in phase with the clock, all is well, but when they drift out of phase, they may experience insomnia at night and sleepiness during the day .","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m8-1-h03","text":"Jet Lag"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A disruption of circadian rhythms after crossing time zones is known as jet lag .","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Travelers complain of sleepiness during the day, sleeplessness at night, and sometimes depression and impaired concentration .","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most people find it easier to adjust to crossing time zones going west than east.","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Going west, we stay awake later at night and then awaken late the next morning, already partly adjusted to the new schedule.","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stress elevates blood levels of the adrenal hormone cortisol , and prolonged elevation of cortisol damages neurons in the hippocampus, an area important for memory.","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One study examined flight attendants who had spent the previous 5 years making flights across seven or more time zones—such as Chicago to Italy— usually having breaks of fewer than 6 days between trips.","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"These results suggest a danger from repeated adjustments of the circadian rhythm, although the problem here could be air travel itself.","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m8-1-h04","text":"Night Work"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People who work on a night shift, such as midnight to 8 a.m., sleep during the day.","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"On average, night-shift workers have more accidents than day-shift workers.","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It is difficult to adjust the circadian rhythm to work at night, because most buildings use artificial lighting in the range of 150 to 180 lux, which is only moderately effective in resetting the rhythm .","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People adjust better if they sleep in a very dark room during the day and work under very bright lights at night, comparable to the noonday sun .","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Short-wavelength (bluish) light resets the circadian rhythm more strongly than long-wavelength light does .","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m8-1-h05","text":"Morning People and Evening People"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Some people (“morning people” or “larks”) awaken early, reach their peak of productivity early, and become less alert later.","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Others (“evening people” or “owls”) warm up slowly, both literally and figuratively, reaching their peak in the late afternoon or evening.","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"shift workers, morning people are most impaired when working the night shift and evening people are most impaired when working the morning shift .","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The tendency to stay up later during adolescence occurs in every culture that researchers have studied throughout the world .","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"From a functional standpoint, we can only speculate as to why staying up late and waking up late might be more advantageous for adolescents than for children or adults.","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In low-tech societies without electric lights, people go to sleep about three hours after sunset, seldom awaken during the night, and wake up at sunrise.","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Those who are strongly evening types tend to get lower than average test scores, especially in their morning classes .","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In both adolescence and adulthood, morning people report being happier than evening people, on average, at least partly because their biological rhythms are more in tune with their school or work schedule .","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m8-1-h06","text":"Mechanisms of the Biological Clock"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Curt Richter first demonstrated that the brain generates its own rhythms—a biological clock—and he found that the biological clock is insensitive to most forms of interference.","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Blind or deaf animals generate circadian rhythms, although they slowly drift out of phase with the external world.","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The circadian rhythm remains surprisingly steady despite food or water deprivation, X-rays, tranquilizers, alcohol, anesthesia, lack of oxygen, most kinds of brain damage, or the removal of endocrine organs.","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"or more of induced hibernation often fails to reset the biological clock .","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Evidently, the biological clock is a hardy, robust mechanism.","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m8-1-h07","text":"The Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (SCN)"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although cells throughout the body generate circadian rhythms, the main driver of rhythms for sleep and body temperature is the suprachiasmatic (soo-pruh-kie-as-MAT-ik) nucleus , or SCN , a part of the hypothalamus .","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It gets its name from its location just above (“supra”) the optic chiasm (Figure 8.7).","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If SCN neurons are disconnected from the rest of the brain or removed from the body and maintained in tissue culture, they continue to produce a circadian rhythm of action potentials .","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A single SCN cell can maintain a circadian rhythm, but not very accurately.","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A mutation in one gene causes hamsters’ SCN to produce a 20-hour instead of 24-hour rhythm .","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers surgically removed the SCN from adult hamsters and transplanted SCN tissue from hamster fetuses into the adults.","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When they transplanted SCN tissue from fetuses with a 20-hour rhythm, the recipients produced a 20-hour rhythm.","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m8-1-h08","text":"How Light Resets the SCN"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Mice with genetic defects that destroy nearly all their rods and cones nevertheless respond to light by resetting their biological clocks .","sourcePrintedPage":264,"sourcePdfPage":282,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Nevertheless, light resets their circadian rhythms, enabling them to be awake only at night .","sourcePrintedPage":264,"sourcePdfPage":282,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The explanation is that the retinohypothalamic path to the SCN comes from certain retinal ganglion cells that have their own photopigment, melanopsin .","sourcePrintedPage":264,"sourcePdfPage":282,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"These special ganglion cells receive some input from rods and cones , but even without that input, they respond directly to light .","sourcePrintedPage":264,"sourcePdfPage":282,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because they respond slowly when light comes on and decline slowly when the light ceases, they respond to the overall average amount of light, not to instantaneous changes in light .","sourcePrintedPage":265,"sourcePdfPage":283,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because television, video games, computers, and eReaders emit mostly short-wavelength light, late-evening exposure to them phase-delays the circadian rhythm, makes it difficult to fall asleep, and impairs alertness the next morning .","sourcePrintedPage":265,"sourcePdfPage":283,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m8-1-h09","text":"Biochemistry of the Circadian Rhythm"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Research on production of the circadian rhythm began when studies on the fruit fly Drosophila found genes that produce a circadian rhythm .","sourcePrintedPage":265,"sourcePdfPage":283,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the feedback cycle takes about 24 hours, a fly can generate a circadian rhythm even in an unchanging environment.","sourcePrintedPage":265,"sourcePdfPage":283,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, in addition to the automatic feedback, light activates a chemical that breaks down the TIM protein about as fast as it forms during the day (as represented in the figure), keeping the fly awake.","sourcePrintedPage":265,"sourcePdfPage":283,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The reason is that analyzing the mechanism in flies told researchers what to look for in humans and other mammals.","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with certain PER mutations have a circadian rhythm shorter than 24 hours, as if they were moving about a time zone east every day .","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Other genetic mutations can cause the reverse condition, a circadian rhythm longer than 24 hours, marked by difficulty waking up on time in the morning .","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m8-1-h10","text":"Melatonin"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The suprachiasmatic nucleus regulates waking and sleeping by controlling activity levels in other brain areas, including the pineal gland (PIN-ee-al; Figure 8.7), an endocrine gland located just posterior to the thalamus .","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Melatonin is a widespread chemical, found in nearly all animals—sponges are the only known exception—as well as in plants and bacteria.","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People who have pineal gland tumors sometimes stay awake for days at a time .","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In addition to regulating sleep and wakefulness, melatonin also helps control the onset of puberty and adjustments to changes of season, such as hibernation.","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Taking a melatonin pill in the evening has little effect on sleepiness because the pineal gland produces melatonin at that time anyway.","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Taking melatonin earlier can hasten the onset of sleepiness and shift the circadian rhythm .","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Melatonin pills are sometimes helpful when people travel across time zones and need to sleep at an unaccustomed time.","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m8-1-h11","text":"In Closing: Sleep–Wake Cycles"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike an electric appliance that stays on until someone turns it off, the brain periodically turns itself on and off.","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Our biological mechanisms prepare us to wake at certain times and sleep at other times, even if we would prefer other schedules.","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"In some way their brain is keeping track of the date to generate an endogenous circannual rhythm.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":258,"sourcePdfPage":276},{"type":"bullet","text":"( Endogenous means “generated from within.” Circannual comes from the Latin words circum, for “about,” and annum, for “year.”) Animals also produce endogenous circadian rhythms that last about a day.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":258,"sourcePdfPage":276},{"type":"bullet","text":"Our circadian rhythm does not easily adjust to more severe departures from a 24-hour schedule.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277},{"type":"bullet","text":"Naval personnel on submarines are cut off from sunlight for months at a time, living under artificial light.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277},{"type":"bullet","text":"These results suggest a biologically driven circadian rhythm in emotional well-being.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277},{"type":"bullet","text":"Unless something resets your circadian rhythm, it would gradually drift away from the correct time.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277},{"type":"bullet","text":"The stimulus that resets your circadian rhythm is referred to by the German term zeitgeber (TSITE-gay-ber), meaning “time-giver.” Light is by far the dominant zeitgeber for land animals, whereas the tides are important for some marine animals.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":259,"sourcePdfPage":277},{"type":"bullet","text":"As a result, they are not fully alert during their wakeful periods or deeply asleep during rest periods.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":260,"sourcePdfPage":278},{"type":"bullet","text":"You set your clock to an hour later, and when it shows your usual bedtime, you dutifully go to bed, even though it seems an hour too early.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":260,"sourcePdfPage":278},{"type":"bullet","text":"In fall, when daylight saving time ends, some people have sleep problems then, too.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":260,"sourcePdfPage":278},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, if on weekends and holidays you prefer to go to bed at 12:30 a.m. and awaken at 8:30 a.m., your sleep midpoint is 4:30 a.m.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":260,"sourcePdfPage":278},{"type":"bullet","text":"Most people find it difficult to go to sleep before their body’s usual time and difficult to wake up early the next day.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279},{"type":"bullet","text":"On the average, the flight attendants had smaller than average volumes of the hippocampus and surrounding structures, and they showed memory impairments.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":261,"sourcePdfPage":279},{"type":"bullet","text":"They tolerate staying up all night better than morning people do.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280},{"type":"bullet","text":"A convenient way to classify people is to ask, “On holidays and vacations when you have no obligations, what time is the middle of your sleep?” For example, if you sleep from 1 a.m. until 9 a.m. on those days, your middle is 5 a.m.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280},{"type":"bullet","text":"So, being a “morning person” or an “evening person” depends partly on age.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":262,"sourcePdfPage":280},{"type":"bullet","text":"After a society gains electric lights, people stay awake later and get less sleep.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281},{"type":"bullet","text":"The tendency for most young people to be evening types causes problems.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281},{"type":"bullet","text":"After damage to the SCN, the body’s rhythms become erratic.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281},{"type":"bullet","text":"That is, the rhythm followed the pace of the donors, not the recipients.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281},{"type":"bullet","text":"The illustration shows the position of the SCN in the human brain, just above the optic chiasm.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":263,"sourcePdfPage":281},{"type":"bullet","text":"Most of the input to that path does not come from normal retinal receptors.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":264,"sourcePdfPage":282},{"type":"bullet","text":"Also, consider blind mole rats, whose eyes are covered with folds of skin and fur.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":264,"sourcePdfPage":282},{"type":"bullet","text":"The average intensity is exactly the information the SCN needs to gauge the time of day.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":265,"sourcePdfPage":283},{"type":"bullet","text":"A flash of lightning in the middle of the night does not mean that daytime has arrived.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":265,"sourcePdfPage":283},{"type":"bullet","text":"Two of these genes, known as period (abbreviated PER ) and timeless ( TIM ), produce the proteins PER and TIM.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":265,"sourcePdfPage":283},{"type":"bullet","text":"The concentration of these proteins, which promote sleep, oscillates over a day, based on feedback interactions.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":265,"sourcePdfPage":283},{"type":"bullet","text":"They consistently get sleepy early in the evening and awaken early in the morning.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284},{"type":"bullet","text":"People with an altered PER gene look forward to times when they can go to bed early.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284},{"type":"bullet","text":"Melatonin secretion starts to increase about 2 or 3 hours before bedtime.","headingId":"bp14-m8-1-h10","sourcePrintedPage":266,"sourcePdfPage":284}],"topicIds":["bp14-m8-1-h01","bp14-m8-1-h02","bp14-m8-1-h03","bp14-m8-1-h04","bp14-m8-1-h05","bp14-m8-1-h06","bp14-m8-1-h07","bp14-m8-1-h08","bp14-m8-1-h09","bp14-m8-1-h10","bp14-m8-1-h11"],"studySections":[{"id":"bp14-m8-1-study-1","title":"Biological rhythms are built in","text":"Many bodily processes vary across roughly daily cycles, including alertness, hormone secretion, and temperature. Circadian rhythms are endogenous, meaning they can continue even when ordinary external time cues are absent. Nonetheless, light and daily routines help reset them to the environment. The distinction between an internal oscillator and an outside cue is essential: light usually synchronizes a system rather than creating each individual rhythm from nothing.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":258,"sourcePrintedEnd":268,"sourcePdfStart":276,"sourcePdfEnd":286},{"id":"bp14-m8-1-study-2","title":"The suprachiasmatic nucleus","text":"A small hypothalamic region called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) acts as a central circadian timing system in mammals. Input related to environmental light helps adjust its timing. Molecular feedback mechanisms inside cells support recurring rhythms, and the SCN influences other neural and hormonal processes. Melatonin is associated with the night phase and can convey timing information, but it is not a substitute for understanding the whole clock system.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":258,"sourcePrintedEnd":268,"sourcePdfStart":276,"sourcePdfEnd":286},{"id":"bp14-m8-1-study-3","title":"Jet lag, shift work, and chronotype","text":"Travel across time zones may abruptly change the clock time outside while internal rhythms remain closer to the old schedule. The resulting mismatch is jet lag. Night work can similarly put sleep and activity out of step with some biological timing processes. Individuals differ in whether they naturally prefer earlier or later schedules, often described as morningness and eveningness. These variations make sleep timing a biological as well as a practical issue.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":258,"sourcePrintedEnd":268,"sourcePdfStart":276,"sourcePdfEnd":286},{"id":"bp14-m8-1-study-4","title":"What to remember about resetting","text":"Light exposure at different times can shift the circadian clock in different directions, so timing matters as much as amount. Other routines may contribute to synchronization, but light is a major signal. Do not confuse total hours slept with circadian alignment: a person can sleep for an adequate duration but at a biologically awkward time and still experience problems with alertness.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":258,"sourcePrintedEnd":268,"sourcePdfStart":276,"sourcePdfEnd":286}],"contentLevel":"verified_hierarchical_topic_notes_and_module_explanations","selfCheck":[{"question":"Can you explain: Biological rhythms are built in?","answer":"Many bodily processes vary across roughly daily cycles, including alertness, hormone secretion, and temperature.
